chapters.summary: Shaun Abreu introduces Father Khader El-Yateem of Grace Lutheran Church of Brooklyn, who delivers an invocation praying for wisdom, courage, and justice for the city and its leaders.
chapters.title: Invocation delivered by Father Khader El-Yateem

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now have today's invocation, which will be delivered by Father Khare Kalili of Grace Lutheran Church of Brooklyn, which is located at 939 3rd Street in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Let us pray.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Almighty and merciful God, you created each of us in your image, the people in this chamber, the people watching from home,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: and even those who will never hear our names, but whose lives are shaped by the decisions made here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: We thank you for this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: We thank you for the people of the Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens, and Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: We thank you for its crowded trains, its busy neighborhoods, its hardworking families, and its stubborn habit of making room for one more person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: In Jesus, you showed us what it means not to be served, but to serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Let that same spirit fill this room today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Bless the members of this council and all who serve alongside them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Give them wisdom when the answers are unclear, and courage when the right choice comes at a cost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Help them listen to one another,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: especially to those with whom they disagree, and leave them to see

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: not the good of a few, but the common good of all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Through the prophet Micah, you have shown us what is good, to do justice, to love kindness, and to walk humbly with you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Keep before the minds and hearts of this city, of this council, the family struggling to pay the rent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: The workers striving to make ends meet, the child who goes to school hungry, and the elder living alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Make them faithful stewards of the trust placed in them, and give peace in this nation, peace in our city, peace in our homes, and peace in our hearts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Though we pray these things by different names, I offer this prayer in the name of Jesus Christ, trusting that we stand together in the hope of your mercy and goodness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Father Khader El-Yateem
utterances.text: Amen.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin delivers her communication, focusing on the 19-year effort to ban horse-drawn carriages. She thanks Romancia's family, advocates, and colleagues, and announces the passage of Romancia's law.
chapters.title: Speaker Julie Menin announces passage of Romancia's law and honors family

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now have communication from Speaker Julie Menon.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Majority Leader, and I want to thank everyone for joining us today in the chambers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For 19 years, the City Council has considered a ban on the horse carriage industry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In fact, it was 19 years ago that the first City Council bill on this issue was actually introduced in these chambers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, we are converting consideration into action.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For 19 years, a solution has been delayed and promises went unfulfilled.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, we plan to deliver on all fronts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And for 19 years, we've debated the issue without an outcome.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: All the while, while horse-drawn carriage was sadly in June involved in a tragic

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today we prevent the next one, passing Romancia's law and the process, and I want to thank Romancia's family and ask them to please stand up.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know your unimaginable pain and grief, and we know that by passing Romancia's law, it is a lasting legacy in his honor.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we really thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are many parties to thank for the success of these efforts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have NICLAS and PETA, countless advocates and community leaders.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Most importantly, I want to thank our city council colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: For their thoughtful, intentional ways that they have gone about proposing, sponsoring, amending, and soon voting on this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to thank the bill sponsor, Councilmember Marte, for all of his hard work on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to thank the health chair, Councilmember Shulman, for her work.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You're getting applause on this issue and all of the colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I also want to acknowledge and thank those who came before us in the council for their hard work in this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have with us today former council member Bob Holden, who was a major leader in the fight, having first introduced riders law in 2022.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you, Bob.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And earlier, I don't know if he's still here, but earlier, ah, okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There's Rob, hello.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And earlier, former council member Tony Avella, who introduced that first bill 19 years ago, was here as well.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin details the horse carriage phase-out set for June 2028, humane treatment requirements for horses, worker transition programs, and consideration of compensation for medallion owners.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines provisions of Romancia's law

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Romant's law will do justice to this effort in more ways than one.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It sets a June 2028 phase-out deadline, which supports the principles of public safety so that Romant is the last soul that we lose to this industry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It is going to ensure that the horses themselves receive humane treatment wherever they go next.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Requiring certification that horses will not be transferred for slaughter.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But it does, and I want to be clear about this, and this is very important, it allows the horse owners to keep their horses if they choose, because that is very important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we heard powerful testimony at our hearing on that topic.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And it is going to support the transition for the more than 150 active horse carriage drivers, helping them to find new jobs over the next two years.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And that is incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This city council beefed up the worker protection language because we want to ensure

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: that we are working to make sure that these workers have meaningful, gainful employment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Under the bill, it includes providing civil service trainings, career counseling, assistance, accessing education, referrals to other...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: employment opportunities and this City Council will work very closely with the administration to ensure that those workers have those jobs because that's what they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because whether they're medallion owners, which we also want to protect, based in the stables or driving the carriages themselves, these workers all call our city home and they deserve to keep working, growing and thriving in our city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill also requires the administration to consider establishing a compensation program, and the council is very committed to working with the administration throughout this transition period.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Passing this law proves not simply that we are committed to making our city safer and more livable for residents, tourists, and animals alike.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It proves that we can live up to the commitments that we make.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin discusses the homeowner expo with Deputy Speaker Williams, the expansion of free 2K to the Bronx and Staten Island, a hearing on EMS response times, the Champions Plaza street co-naming, and the vote to raise SCRI/DRI income eligibility to $75,000.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin highlights council initiatives: homeowner expo, 2K, EMS, SCRI/DRI

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: There are other ways that we in the council are bringing our commitments to fruition as well.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So switching gears, on Saturday, I joined our deputy speaker, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Nantasha Williams.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We went to York College for our first installment of our homeowner expo.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Residents Access 101 consulting on how to protect their homes from threats such as predatory loans, deed theft, storm damage, foreclosure.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The event was a part of our $5.5 million commitment to our new homeowner stabilization services.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: which will help residents preserve their homes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we'll be going to every single borough on this tour.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On Monday, I was proud to join the mayor and the governor to announce that free 2K will be available to every school district in the Bronx and Staten Island by the fall of 2027.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That expansion means an additional 10,000 children will have a shot at a brighter future, and thousands more parents won't have to empty their pockets to pay for child care.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And on that note, this city council has passed so many bills and will continue to do so to make it easier to operate child care facilities, to cut down on the bureaucracy necessary to open them.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have passed an enormous amount of bills in that regard and more to come.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And we're also very proud of the fact that in 2022, this city council passed the Universal Child Act, becoming the first city across the country to set universal child care as a goal.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On Tuesday, we held a hearing on the response times of our EMS services.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The department is severely underfunded, leading to inadequate staffing that poses deadly consequences.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Currently, a New Yorker must wait, on average, 13 minutes and 9 seconds for EMS to arrive.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 13 minutes and 9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know that after four months,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: minutes is when brain cells start to die if someone is deprived of oxygen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is completely and wholly unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So every single minute alone matters.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We must pay those who provide a life-saving service a living wage and ensure that New Yorkers in crisis can access the care that they need.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: On a lighter note, ahead of the opening night for the Knicks, we unveiled a street co-naming, Champions Plaza, in honor of these...

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yes, applause over there.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In honor of the seven championships won between our home teams, the Knicks and the Rangers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Obviously, it didn't go New York's way on Tuesday, but today is a different day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the City Council certainly has plenty of victories to celebrate on behalf of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So on that note, today we'll be voting on raising the income eligibility limit to $75,000 for the Senior Citizen Rent Increase, SCRI.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And the Disability Rent Increase Exemption Program, DRE.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is a truly meaningful difference from the current cap of $50,000, which it has been since 2019.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you to Councilmember Lewis for her important work on this very important legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This program, which freezes rent for eligible senior citizens and disabled New Yorkers while still giving landlords a tax credit, will provide major relief to those

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: residents, assuring that they can stay in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's just one of the many initiatives the council has proposed to make New York City affordable and livable for everyone.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin acknowledges Hindu festivals, Filipino American, Polish American, and Disability Employment Awareness Months, honors first responders, wishes a happy Halloween, encourages voting on Election Day, and welcomes One Strong Brotherhood.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin recognizes heritage months, first responders, and welcomes guests

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Switching gears a little, this month the Hindu community is celebrating

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Nuvratri, Endura Japaiju, and Dasara.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These connected festivals honor the triumph of good over evil and the divine feminine.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: However you celebrated, I hope your observance was joyful and meaningful.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: October is Filipino American Heritage Month.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: In October of 1587, the first Filipinos arrived in our nation in what is now California.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Almost 500 years later, we are proud to have almost 100,000 Filipino Americans who call this city their home, from Little Manila and Woodside to those who work in every industry of our city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It's also Polish American Heritage Month and the month that General Kazimierz Pulaski died, giving his life to the American Revolution two years after saving George Washington's.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The Polish population in this city has expanded greatly since, and their presence and their contributions are everywhere, from churches in Greenpoint to pierogies in our restaurants,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: and we're very proud to celebrate that heritage.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: National Disability Employment Awareness Month is also observed every October to celebrate workers with disabilities and promote inclusive workplace practices.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Almost one million people in our city have a disability, and hundreds of thousands of them are employed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: That's why I was very proud as Speaker that we created the first disability committee, a committee dedicated to this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will continue to ensure that all New Yorkers can work and keep a job.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: October 28th is National First Responders Day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We will honor the brave people across our five boroughs who protect us, to our firefighters, our police officers, our EMTs, our paramedics, and 9-11 dispatchers.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much for everything you're doing every single day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We at the council will continue to fight so that you all can receive the compensation you deserve.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: October 31st is Halloween, so let me just on a lighter note wish everyone a happy Halloween.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And November 3rd is Election Day, so please make a plan to vote and alert your neighbors, friends, and family.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to give a warm welcome to One Strong Brotherhood, who is here with Councilmember Kevin Riley.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: First Councilmember Riley.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We want to give a warm welcome.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We're honoring them today for their contributions to uplifting young black men, and I'm told that you all have quite the Instagram following.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Word has it.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Finally, I want to wish a happy birthday to Councilmember Phil Wong, who celebrated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Happy birthday.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: To Councilmember Vicky Palladino, who will celebrate on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And to Councilmember Oswald Feliz, who will celebrate on the 29th.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now we will move on to our stated agenda.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin lists three land use items: 48-50 Convent Avenue Cluster ANCP for affordable homeownership, 1455 Coney Island Avenue rezoning for a long-term care facility, and 135-27 Sapphire Street rezoning for a six-story building with affordable units.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines land use items for vote

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: First, we'll vote on the following land use items.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 48-50 Convent Avenue Cluster ANCP will support the conversion of four partially occupied city-owned rental buildings to 77

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: affordable homeownership units and two superintendent units under the Affordable Housing Cooperative Program and Majority Leader Sean Abreu's district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 1455 Coney Island Avenue rezoning will facilitate the development of nine-story long-term facility with 300 patient beds in Councilmember Simca Felder's district.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 135-27 Sapphire Street rezoning will facilitate the development of one

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: six-story building with approximately 268 dwelling units, 67 to 80 of which will be affordable under MIH in Councilmember Joanne Areola's district.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin lists finance items: Intro 978B to increase SCRI/DRI income limit to $75,000, Resolution 666-A for BID expenditures, a transparency resolution, and pre-considered resolutions for 40-year tax exemptions.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines finance items for vote

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Next, we'll vote on the following finance items.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 978B, also sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would increase the maximum income level for eligibility for SCRI and DRI to $75,000 beginning July 1, 2026.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 666-A, sponsored by Councilmember Linda Lee, would set the date, time, and place for the hearing of the local law that would increase the annual expenditure for eight business improvement districts.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: A transparency resolution approving new designations and changes in the designation of certain organizations receiving funding in the expense budget.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And several pre-considered resolutions sponsored by Councilmember Linda Lee as well that would grant a partial 40-year tax

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: exemption under Article 11 of the Private Housing Finance Law for buildings in the districts of Councilmembers Wilson and Carnesian, Feliz, Justin Sanchez, and Deputy Speaker Williams.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin lists Resolution 625B for Reggaeton Heritage Month, Resolution 650 opposing federal Head Start rule changes, Intro 927 renaming Shorefront Parkway, Intro 797A on voter registration in jails, and Intro 853A on special education access.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines legislation: resolutions and intros on ballots, street renaming, special ed

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Today, we will also vote on the following pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 625B, sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would declare October as Reggaeton Heritage Month in the City of New York to honor its legacy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to our staff, Regina Paul.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Resolution 650, sponsored by Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez, would oppose a federally proposed rule change titled

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs and call on the federal government to prioritize protecting and growing access to high-quality education for young children.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Katie Selena and Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 927, sponsored by Councilmember Selena Brooks-Powers, would rename Shorefront.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Parkway between Beach 32nd Street and Beach 56th Place to Edgemere Avenue and amend the official city map accordingly.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Chris Sartori, Patrick Mulvihill, and Owen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Katawski.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 797A, sponsored by public advocate Jumaane Williams, would require DOC, in addition to semi-annual reporting on voter registration forms,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to annually report on the number of voter registration and voting activities in city jails, as well as on demographic information for people returning voter registration forms to DOC.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Jahari Frazier and Chad Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 853A, sponsored by Councilmember Susan Chuang, would require the DOE to supplement existing special education reporting

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: with analysis on how geographic location, home language, and household income affect students'access to special ed programs and services and to report recommendations and how to address any

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: identified barriers to access.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Alejandro Carjavel.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin describes Intro 905A (COPA) giving nonprofits first opportunity to purchase distressed properties, Intro 786A requiring procedures for curing ballots in DOC custody, and Intro 296A requiring reports on gender-based violence data.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines legislation: COPA, ballot curing, gender-based violence data

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 905A, sponsored by Councilmember Sandy Nurse, would give certain not-for-profits or joint ventures between not-for-profits and other entities

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: a first opportunity to submit a statement of interest in purchasing and a first opportunity to purchase certain residential properties when offered for sale.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Austin Malone, William A.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Jose Conde and Dirk Spencer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 786-A, sponsored by Councilmember Savina Brooks-Powers, would require the Commissioner of Corrections to create procedures for curing ballots for voters in DOC custody.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Jahari Frazier and to Chad Benjamin.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Introduction 296-A, sponsored by Councilmember Farrah Lewis, would require the Mayor's Office to end gender-based violence in consultation with the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: to develop a report with recommendations for agencies to improve the collection and integration of data on gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill would also require the offices to develop an outreach program to survey health care providers about screening practices for gender-based violence and provide support to integrate trauma-informed practice into the screenings.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill would require NGBV to develop a data dashboard to share data from city and state agencies around gender-based violence in the city.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Finally, the bill would require DHS and ACS to report some information about screenings that they are conducting, including the number of screenings that led to services or referrals for gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Julia Goldsmith-Pinkham and to Katie Salina.

chapters.summary: Speaker Menin details Intro 943A, which winds down the horse-drawn cab industry by prohibiting new licenses after June 1, 2028, requiring humane disposition of horses, and establishing a transition plan for workers and owners.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin outlines horse carriage bill (Intro 943A)

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And lastly, introduction 9-4.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 3-A, sponsored by Councilmember Marche, would wind down the horse-drawn cab industry by prohibiting the issuance of licenses for carriage horses, horse-drawn cabs, and horse-drawn cab drivers

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: on or after June 1, 2028.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Any licenses active as of the effective date of the bill would permanently expire on May 31, 2028.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This bill requires the humane disposition of carriage horses and prohibits their sale or transfer for inhumane purposes, such as for slaughter or for use in another horse-drawn cab business.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The bill would also require an agency or agencies designated by the mayor to establish a horse-drawn cab industry transition plan by April 1, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The plan would include a workforce transition program, consideration of a program to assist

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: carriage horse owners with the disposition of their horses and equipment, and consideration of a program to provide compensation to horse-drawn cab owners for the value of their business licenses and equipment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you to Christopher Pepe, Elizabeth Arts, Joshua Newman, Elliot Lin, Sahar Mozami, and Smita Deshmukh.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your attention to us.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Now I'll turn it back over to our majority leader.

chapters.summary: Council Member James Gennaro moves to amend Intro 943A to extend the effective date to January 1, 2030. He argues workers need more time to transition and that the bill lacks concrete commitments for their livelihoods.
chapters.title: Council Member Gennaro proposes amendment to extend horse carriage phase-out to 2030

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker Menon.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now move into discussion of general orders.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I recognize Councilmember Gennaro, who wishes to speak on some matters.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I move to amend Intro 943A.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I think the best description of the...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Of the amendment I was told would come from the parliamentarian.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: If you could explain to the members what this amendment would do.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: I don't think the clock should be running until the amendment is explained to the members.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Anyone else would like to speak on the amendment being proposed?

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But we don't know what it is yet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The motion to amend is the following.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A yes will extend effective date to January 1st, 2030 as part of Section 17-327A2.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And if we vote on this amendment, it will lay over Intro 943A for the next stated for a vote.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A no vote will leave Intro 943A unchanged and we will vote on it today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Anyone who wishes, we can now go to roll call.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Anyone who wishes to speak has two minutes to speak.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: But I speak for you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: General, you may finish your time.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council member, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: When we were listening to Father Kalilia, he made mention in his benediction, he talked about drivers working to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That was part of his blessing.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And I think, I don't think anyone wants to see the drivers in this good industry put upon in such a way that they will be unable to feed their families.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And as the bill stands now, we would receive, or they would receive, the city would receive

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: a document from the mayor, a plan that would take care of the disposition of the horses, the disposition of the workers into new jobs, and the disposition of the medallions.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Understanding that, you know, the language associated with that is, will consider reimbursement, consider, it's a pig in a poke.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Like, I get it.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so this is how it's playing out.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: The drivers were promised, the city was promised that...

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: The program for the workers, for the drivers, for the medallion owners, to quote the speaker on 7-16-26, we need to do more to protect the workers.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: We're really trying to come up with more robust language, which I think needs to be inserted into that bill.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That never actually happened.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And so what I'm really asking for is if this thing comes out on April 1st like it's supposed to, then the industry's got 14 months to pack up because they don't know what is going to be in that.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: They don't know what's going to be in that report.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: And what I'm asking for is give them an extra 18 months to figure out their lives because they were supposed to have today what they need.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: So they know what's going to become of them.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: That won't exist at best until April 1st of 2001.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano opposes the amendment, arguing that the industry has had decades to prepare and that delaying the vote would reinforce political cynicism. He urges colleagues to vote on the bill without amendment today.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano urges vote against amendment, calls for immediate vote

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You got it.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, we have Councilor Marano followed by Palladino speaking specifically on the amendment being proposed.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I appreciate my colleague putting forth such a thoughtful amendment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I would urge all of my colleagues, irrespective of...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: of how you feel about the bill to ban horse-drawn carriages to vote against this amendment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As the Speaker chronicled, we have had two decades of discussion and debate about this, and the bill as it stands now gives 18 months for

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: the drivers to figure out their next step.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I'm all about preserving history.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Preserving history doesn't mean maintaining every practice that's ever existed throughout history.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There was a time when being a lamplighter in New York City was a lucrative job, or an elevator operator, or an ice man.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the people, the hardworking people that had those jobs, didn't have the luxury of a two-year warning that they were not going to have those jobs anymore.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So to kick this can down the road for one more stated meeting until we vote, when...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Honestly, I think all of us have spent a lot of time thinking about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those of us that were in the hearing, wherever we end up on the issue, we spent a lot of time listening to testimony about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: To me, we need to vote on this today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: However you feel about it, we need to vote on this without amendment today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: People have waited two decades.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I have a lot of friends and colleagues that are going to vote differently than the way I'm going to vote today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I respect their view, and I understand why.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But to kick this can down the road when we've been doing this for decades, I think it...

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It reinforces everything that makes people so cynical about politics and politicians.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's vote today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're for banning the horse-drawn carriages, vote for it today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you're not, vote no.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's do it today without amendment.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers.

chapters.summary: Council Member Vickie Paladino supports the amendment to extend the deadline, arguing the bill was rushed and that the real danger in parks comes from unlicensed scooters and bicycles. She questions the number of fatalities caused by horse carriages.
chapters.title: Council Member Paladino supports extension, criticizes rushed process

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilor Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Well, as usual, you would expect me to disagree, and I wholeheartedly disagree, and I most definitely agree with Councilmember Gennaro's extension of time.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This was done so hastily, and my condolences to the family, and I'm really sorry that you're

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: being put up here as some sort of token to show the city of New York that one person was killed by a horse.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: When I did my press conference yesterday, it was completely and absolutely about the horse owners

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: and the time and the effort that is put into the horses by the horse owners who have made this generational.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Now, we heard here today 19 years.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Show me the proof that this has been going on for 19 years.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And why doesn't this council really try to figure out what the real danger is in this park, and that is unlicensed, unregistered, and uninsured

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: two-wheel scooters and bicycles that are going through our parks like this.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We also had a speaker there yesterday at the press conference that spoke as a stable owner who proved that you have a $100 million

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: lawsuit, the family, against the city of New York because it was Con Edison's fault that there was a shortage that caused your son to be thrown from the horse.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I want a list of how many people were actually killed by horse-drawn carriages.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The fact that not enough time was given to this bill to allow the horse owners to follow through with their proposal, which was offered to them two years ago, I understand, which they turned down.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Two years, a lot have changed.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Lots of things have changed.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And now they have a proposal to put forward to this city government.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And yet the city will not use...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please mute her mic.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm holding a strict, if you don't speak, peon your time today.

chapters.summary: Council Member Joann Ariola aligns with Paladino, arguing for extended time for horse owners and warning that if the referendum passes, other industries could be targeted next.
chapters.title: Council Member Ariola supports extension, warns of precedent

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, anyone else would like to speak on the amendments today?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, Councilmember Areola.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I do align myself with the comments made by my colleague, Vicki Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: There should be an extended time because we only have what ifs for the horse owners, for their horses, and for their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I say further to all of you here in this chamber, what if...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In November, on November 3rd, the referendums pass, and they start to excise us as they're trying to do.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Who will be next?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: What industry will be targeted next?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's what we have to look at.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Not what happened 19 years ago, but what's happening now, because it will define what happens in the future.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for the time, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Speaker Menon, would you like to make remarks?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Or is...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin addresses Romancia's family, apologizing for any suggestion that they were being used and expressing condolences for their loss.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin apologizes to Romancia's family

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm happy to make remarks.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to say to Ramach's family, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You came here because you are mourning the loss of Ramach.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You came here for that reason.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You asked to come here, and we wanted to honor your request to be here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so I'm sorry if anyone would suggest anything but that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: It is a terrible tragedy we went through, that you went through, and our hearts are with you.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I wanted to mention that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right, I just want to remind folks of the motion being voted on today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The motion to amend is the following.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A yes vote will extend effective date to January 1st, 2030 as part of Section 17-327A2 and lay over Intro 943A for next stated for a vote.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: A no vote will leave Intro 943A unchanged and we will vote on it today.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As a reminder, for folks who are voting, you have two minutes to speak, if you would like to speak on your vote.

chapters.summary: The Council conducts a roll call vote on Council Member Gennaro's amendment to extend the effective date of Intro 943A to January 1, 2030. During the roll call, Council Members Brewer, Gennaro, and Marte explain their votes. The amendment is defeated by a vote of 6 in favor and 43 against.
chapters.title: Roll call vote on amendment to extend horse carriage phase-out

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu

chapters.summary: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams speaks in support of Intro 797, which requires the Department of Correction to report annually on voter registration and absentee ballots in city jails. He highlights the disenfranchisement of eligible incarcerated New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Public Advocate Jumaane Williams speaks on Intro 797 for voting in city jails

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And we'll now be resuming the agenda with the general orders discussion, beginning with public advocate Jumaane Williams.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Followed by Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I'm here to speak on an unrelated bill, Intro 797.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: I know many of us are thinking about the South when we think of black and brown voters disenfranchised, but for some of us, we don't have to look that far just into the East River.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker, men and the council for voting on this bill today.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: There are close to 7,000 people detained on Rikers Island, most of them who are eligible to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Though people who have been convicted of felony cannot vote while incarcerated, most people on Rikers are being detained pre-trial or serving time for misdemeanors and therefore are eligible to cast a ballot.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Despite this, only a fraction of the incarcerated population in the jails vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: As the majority of the Rikers population is black and brown, it's hard not to hear the echoes of Jim Crow and this effect of disenfranchisement of thousands of potential voters.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Though volunteers can help people on Rikers register to vote, it is still the responsibility of the BOE and the DOC to deliver absentee ballots to the jail population and to count those completed ballots.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This seems straightforward, but often isn't.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Advocates report that BOE routinely rejects completed registration forms, absentee ballots,

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: requests and complaints.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: completed ballots from eligible incarcerated New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In the outside world, a person's ballot who's rejected would be notified and they would have the opportunity to address any issues.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: The same is often not true of those on Rikers Island.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: In practice, only some of those who requested a ballot receive it, and only some of those ballots are counted, leaving only a small percentage of the eligible population actually able to vote.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: This would not be acceptable in the outside world, and we should not accept it in the right as either.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Today, the City Council is voting on legislation that gives us a better scope of voting landscape inside Rikers.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: My bill, Intro 797, which I co-introduced with Councilmember Brooks Powers, would require the Department of Education to report annually on voter registration inside city jails, including the number of completed voter registration forms,

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: disaggregated by facility and demographic information, as well as the numbers of absentee ballots distributed to incarcerated people.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Civil rights, including voter rights, are not optional.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Just because a person is incarcerated does not mean they do not have a vested interest in their communities, including who represents them in government.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Voting is one of a number of pro-social behaviors associated with reduced recidivism.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: So ensuring that our incarceration population can vote, we should, and I thank everyone in the House.

utterances.speaker: Jumaane Williams
utterances.text: Speaker, Councilman Brooks-Powell, my staff, Veronica Aves, Rosie Mendez, Jeffrey Sivari, and Saffron from my office.

chapters.summary: Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers presents two bills: Intro 927A to rename Shorefront Parkway to Edgemere Avenue, and Intro 786A to improve ballot submission and curing for incarcerated individuals eligible to vote.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I'm proud to have two of my bills before the council today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: First, Intro 927A renames a stretch of Shorefront Parkway back to Edgemere Avenue, as the current name isn't consistently recognized by USPS, Google Maps, and other address systems.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: That corridor will soon be home to Auburn East 1,650 new homes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Second, Intro 786A aims to improve ballot submissions in city jails.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: In less than two weeks, New Yorkers will go to the polls, although many individuals in Department of Correction custody remain eligible to vote.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Participation has historically been extremely low, in part due to challenges in the absentee and early mail ballot systems.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: It is far too easy for a vote to be lost to a missing signature on the ballot envelope, an envelope being incorrectly sealed.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: or a ballot being sent off without the correct envelope.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Intro 786A requires that before the department sends a ballot to the Board of Elections, it must check the envelope that is signed and dated, as well as signed by anyone who helped the voter and actually contains a ballot.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Then the department must give the voter the chance and means to fix any problem.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: These simple fixes aim to increase the number of ballots received and counted by the Board of Elections because being in custody does not end anyone's right to vote.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: A ballot should not be thrown out for an error that could have been caught.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And with that, I ask my colleagues to vote in support of these two pieces of legislation.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member James Gennaro argues that in the 168-year history of the horse carriage industry, no driver has ever had their license revoked or been convicted of animal cruelty. He criticizes the rush to judgment and calls for an oversight hearing instead of a ban.
