chapters.title: Council Member Farah Louis speaks on gender-based violence and rent exemptions

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Farrah Lewis, followed by Marte.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Today we vote on two bills that are about more than policy.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: They are about protecting New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Think of Nathalie Ramirez, a 23-year-old mother who reportedly was pushed from her 15th floor balcony by a former partner.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Her story reminds us that leaving an abusive relationship does not always mean the danger is over.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Intro 296 will help the city better coordinate gender-based violence data, identify gaps, and strengthen prevention so we can intervene before tragedy strikes.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Now think of the senior or disabled New Yorker who has spent years building a life and community in New York only to struggle to afford the home they have lived in for decades.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Intro 978 raises the income eligibility limit for scree and dree from $50,000 to $75,000, helping more eligible older adults and disabled New Yorkers remain in their homes to age with dignity.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: These bills share one purpose, protecting New Yorkers before they fall into the cracks.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to vote on these bills.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councillor Marte, followed by Marano.

chapters.summary: Council Member Christopher Marte, the bill's sponsor, speaks about the 160-year history of the ASPCA and the need to evolve past the horse carriage industry. He honors Romach Mahajan and argues that the city can thrive without legalized animal cruelty.
chapters.title: Council Member Marte speaks on ending horse-drawn carriage industry

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: 160 years ago, the ASPCA was formed right here in New York City, the first national animal welfare organization.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It was started to address one specific issue, the condition of carriage horses in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Now we are here, nearly two centuries later, to complete this mission.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Throughout these years, our city has evolved.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Milkmen no longer deliver milk to our doors.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Construction companies no longer use asbestos or sell asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Paint companies don't sell lead paint.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Pet stores can't sell dogs, cats, rabbits, guinea pigs.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: With every generation, we let go of the past and embrace the future.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Despite the changes in this industry, New York has not just survived, but thrived.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: And we are a city today because we have evolved with the times, and our job as legislator is to guide New York through this evolution.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We've seen the polls.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We see the endless comments on social media.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We see the constant calls and emails we receive from our constituents.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It's beyond clear that New Yorkers are ready for us to evolve past the outdated condition of horse carriage industry in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We can keep Central Park as a destination for millions of New Yorkers and tourists without relying on legalized animal cruelty that puts the public at risk.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: As we all know, this is not a new issue.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Decade after decade, as a list of carriage accidents, dead horses, injured people pile up, elected officials made big promises.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Elections have been decided because of this.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: But it's all been taught.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Despite the promises, nothing has changed, as more horses and people were harmed.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We are guilty of this as well.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: Because of our inaction, Ramash Majan was killed.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: It was unacceptable that it took the tragedy for us to finally pass this bill.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: But this is our opportunity to make sure that Ramash's did not die in vain.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Christopher Marte
utterances.text: We can't, can I please have two seconds?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No, you cannot.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councillor Marano, followed by Nurse.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano speaks against Intro 905A (COPA), arguing it raises constitutional questions about property rights, adds uncertainty to property transactions, and is bad housing policy. He urges colleagues to vote no.
chapters.title: Council Member Morano opposes COPA as unconstitutional and bad housing policy

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: As folks will see, I am making a concerted effort to do something that will upset just about everybody, irrespective of where they fall on the political aisle at some point today.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And at the moment, I rise in strong opposition to an intro 905A, the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act, better known as COPA.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Look, we all agree New York City has an affordability crisis, but giving

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: government-approved organizations special rights in private property sales raises serious constitutional questions, particularly concerning property rights and the limits of municipal authority.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I believe this legislation is totally unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Ultimately, that's a question for the courts, but I think we have a responsibility to confront that here.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I want to address something else.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There's this temptation in politics, and we've all succumbed to it from time to time, to vote for legislation that sounds good, collect the applause, and leave it to a judge to sort out the legal consequences later.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If a court strikes it down, you can tell your supporters you tried.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If it survives, you can claim a victory.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But I don't believe that that's responsible governing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We're legislators, not spectators waiting for the courts to clean up after us.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Even setting aside the constitutional questions, this is terrible housing policy.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: It adds uncertainty to property transactions in a city already struggling to attract investment and produce enough housing.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We should be making it easier to build, easier to rehabilitate neglected properties, and easier for working New Yorkers to afford a home.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Let's stop confusing government intervention with government accomplishment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: More often than not, those are antonyms.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: So I urge my colleagues to vote no on Intro 905A, and let's get to work on real solutions to our affordability crisis.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

chapters.summary: Council Member Sandy Nurse, sponsor of COPA, describes the six-year saga to pass the bill. She explains that COPA lets trusted housing providers buy distressed buildings, keep tenants in their homes at affordable rents, and is a critical anti-displacement tool.
chapters.title: Council Member Nurse urges passage of COPA after six-year effort

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilwoman Nurse, followed by Brewer, then Banks.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Looking forward to Councilman Marano's housing proposals.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Colleagues, today we end the six-year saga.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I'm directing my remarks to the body.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Colleagues, today we end the six-year saga of the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: This has gone through three mayors.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's been introduced four times.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's had three hearings.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's been passed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It's been vetoed.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And it's had a very intense, bad faith lobbying effort to stop it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And it all comes down to today's vote.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We are voting on the most strategic, operationally sound version of this bill.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I believe this thing is solid.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: COPA lets trusted housing providers buy certain buildings, work with tenants, fix those units up, and keep those tenants in their homes at permanently affordable rents.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It is a critical anti-displacement tool, and as one in five New Yorkers say they plan to leave within the next five years because it costs too damn much to live here, today we are offering a chance for families to stay.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: We can not only build our way out of this crisis, if we are serious about stopping displacement, preserving existing housing has to be a priority.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: And that's what COPA does.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: When a building is at risk, the people who live there and the surrounding community get a chance to fight for it.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: It gives eligible landlords a pool of community-oriented buyers who know how to do this work, and it brings those buildings under public oversight.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I really want to thank Speaker Menon for making this a priority.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: I want to thank my colleagues who championed it and those who patiently heard me out.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Many times your input has been extremely invaluable, and because of it, I believe this is a program that the council is going to be able to stand by for years to come.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: So thank you, and I once again ask for your vote for COPA.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandy Nurse
utterances.text: Majority Leader.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer speaks in favor of the SCRI and DRI bills, which help older adults and people with disabilities afford to stay in their homes. She thanks colleagues and says 'yay for old people.'
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer celebrates SCRI and DRI bills for seniors and disabled

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Brewer, followed by Banks.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I just want to say in terms of SCRI and DRI, we all talk about the issue of being able to live in New York affordably, and I have to say these two bills do that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We hear about child care, we hear about the cost of groceries and fuel, but these two bills are really the way to add to the people who are older or who have a disability.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just want to say thank you to all of our colleagues, particularly Council Member Farrah Lewis and everybody, to say yay for old people.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Chris Banks speaks on Intro 943, recognizing Romach Mahajan and arguing that while animal welfare is important, the workers and small business owners in the industry must not be left behind. He calls for real job placement, training, and compensation.
chapters.title: Council Member Banks calls for worker protections in horse carriage transition

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Banks, followed by Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Today, as we consider Introduction 943, that will bring significant change to New York City's horse-drawn carriages industry.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Horse-drawn carriages have long been a part of the character and identity of our city.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Before I discuss the bill, I want to recognize the life of Ramana Mahajian, a young man who tragically lost his life in a horse-drawn carriage accident in Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Our thoughts and prayers remain with his family and the loved ones as they continue to grieve this heartbreaking loss.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: For many New Yorkers, this debate has focused on animal welfare,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This legislation takes important steps to ensure the humane treatment and disposition of carriage horses while establishing a lifeline for the industry's transition.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But at the same time, we cannot lose sight of the workers, the small business owners, the families whose livelihoods depend on this industry.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Many have devoted years and in some cases generations to this profession.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And as we move forward, we must have responsibility to ensure that they are not left behind.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: While the bill requires a transition plan that includes workforce assistance, support for horse owners, and consideration of compensation, those commitments must be more than words on a paper.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We need action.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We need a real job placement opportunities, meaningful workforce training, and support for small business owners.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We must also consider a reimbursement program for those who have made substantial investments in this industry, including medallion owners who have invested hundreds of thousands of dollars.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Strong oversight will be critical in the years ahead.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The council must ensure that the promises made through this legislation translate into real results for the people affected by this transition.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The success of this effort should be measured not only by how the industry changes, but also by how it is.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As a reminder, folks can also speak again during their vote in case if they want to say more.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Palladino, followed by Zhuang.

chapters.summary: Council Member Vickie Paladino speaks against COPA, arguing it infringes on private property rights and will stall sales. She also criticizes the council for killing the horse carriage industry and questions whether members have minds of their own.
chapters.title: Council Member Paladino opposes COPA, criticizes council groupthink

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay, let's cover 905A.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I will be voting no against Intro 905A because the private property owners should have the right to decide when and to whom they sell their own property.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This bill gives designated nonprofits priority in the purchasing process and puts additional restrictions on private sales.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This in itself is very questionable.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The government should not be dictating how the people sell property and how hard they have worked to maintain and own their property.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This bill potentially reduces property value and will stall all sales, which will create unnecessary burdens on the owner.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Private property ownership means something.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And I believe the government has the responsibility to respect these rights for these reasons.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And I also want to go into something else today.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: What a heck of a day in New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We managed to kill an industry.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: That's 160 years old, and we're also managing to kill private home ownership.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You know what?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: When is this group going to finally start to think as individuals and respect?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: their constituents and actually understand and stop this group mentality of thinking and passing what is absolutely ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: COPPA should be a dead issue.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It was brought back out.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And now we're voting on it?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Another thing that's being steamrolled through the city council.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Does anybody in this room have a mind of their own?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Does anybody have a mind of their own?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilman, you're out of order.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I vote no on that.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're not voting yet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Zhuang, followed by Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Council Member Susan Zhuang advocates for Intro 853, which requires an annual study on how geographic location, income, and language affect access to special education. She shares the story of a school bus incident involving nonverbal students.
chapters.title: Council Member Zhuang speaks on Intro 853 for special education access

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Please keep it down in the chambers, please.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also I want to thank Speaker Manning and my colleagues for passing my first bill, first education bill, intro

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: 6884, in my access for all package two weeks ago, expanding equitable access to gifted and talented programs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Today we are voting on its sister bill, intro 853, to help ensure every child can access special education programs they need.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: On December 16, 2025, a school bus carrying six nonverbal special ed students aged from six to eight, even missing for more than four hours.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: As a mother, I cannot imagine the fear those families have.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: suffered.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Too many children in the outborough have to travel long bus rides to reach the service they need.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Meanwhile, language barriers and family income can make it even harder for parents to navigate the system.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We cannot wait to address this inequality issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Intro 853 requires the city to study annually how geographic income and language access affect access to special education programs and services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We need this data to identify the gaps and find solutions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: No child should be left behind because their zip code, their family income, or the language they spoke at home.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Every child deserves access to the education they need to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues, please vote yes on intro.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Council Member Mercedes Narcisse speaks in support of the horse carriage bill, addressing the workers directly. She commits to holding the administration accountable to ensure the transition plan includes jobs, compensation, and care for the horses.
chapters.title: Council Member Narcisse supports horse carriage bill, pledges worker oversight

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Narcisse, and is there anyone else I'm missing for general orders?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If I am missing you, please raise your hand.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority, and thank you, Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Listen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Family of Romage, you just happen to be the catalyst to the process.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We've been going on through this process, and thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The city has debated the future of horse-drawn carriages for many years.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: When Romage died earlier this year, you came here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: for us to make sure that no other family have to go through that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I believe the time is here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I also want to speak to the drivers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Many of you have done this work for decades.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As a small business owner, from a small business owner, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I know we have to do our best, our very best.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And Madam Speaker committed to that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have rent to pay and horses to care for.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And this bill does not yet answer how many get through this.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The bill requires the city hall to deliver a transition plan by April.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I will hold myself accountable and so my colleagues and everyone involved.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If that plan comes back without serious answers on jobs, compensation, and they care for the horses, I will gladly fight alongside TWU Local 100.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: These workers deserve a plan that actually takes care of them, and I will not let a weak one make me regret the vote I cast today.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I support this bill, and I know our work for these workers is not yet finished, and like Madam Speaker said, we'll move forward to make sure we address the workers as well and the families.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Anyone else like to speak on general orders?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Seeing none.

chapters.summary: Council Member Justin Sanchez speaks in support of COPA, highlighting the history of Bronx nonprofit developers like Banana Kelly and Nos Quedamos. He argues COPA will empower community-based organizations to preserve affordable housing.
chapters.title: Council Member Justin Sanchez speaks on COPA and Bronx nonprofit developers

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Justin Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I just want to talk on Councilmember Kavon's bill.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Throughout the history of the Bronx, nonprofit and community-based developers have saved, stabilized, and restored neighborhoods in every corner of our borough.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: When buildings were burning and entire blocks were being abandoned, organizations like Banana Kelly, the Mid-Bronx Esperados, and SEPCO stepped in to rebuild what others had left behind.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: From Charlotte Gardens to Crotona Park East to Kelly Street in Longwood, from the restoration of Morissania Hospital by WETCO to the community-led redevelopment of Melrose by Nos Quedamos, these organizations have done more than build housing.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: They've preserved communities, protected affordable homes, and given generations of Bronx families a reason to stay.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Each of their investments was grounded in their understanding and belief in the community.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA will continue to empower and protect nonprofit developers and allow them to do their critical community building work.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: In a time where private equity firms are buying out housing stock all over the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: And gentrification is running rampant here in New York, we need to use our power as legislators to allow nonprofit developers to keep thriving and stand strong as pillars in our community.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: I'm proud to vote yes on COPA.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA and continue the legacy that these great organizations have built, ensuring that the next generation of community leaders has the tools and opportunities to protect our neighborhoods, preserve affordable housing, and keep the future of the Bronx in the hands of the people to call it home.

utterances.speaker: Justin E. Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Nurse.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Pierina Ana Sanchez explains her vote in favor of COPA, detailing how it targets distressed buildings and gives mission-driven organizations a chance to acquire them. She congratulates Council Member Nurse.
chapters.title: Council Member Pierina Sanchez explains vote on COPA

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Marina Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: New York City is facing a housing crisis, not only because we lack affordable homes, but because too many of the homes we already have are deteriorating under cycles of speculation, disinvestment, and neglect.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Today's vote on Councilmember Nurse's Community Opportunity to Purchase Act gives us a powerful new tool to interrupt those cycles at the point of sale for a limited set of properties.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Those that are between 4 and 100 units that either have an affordability agreement already that is managed by HPD or have a baseline level of physical distress.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: COPA recognizes that the moment a building changes hands is a critical opportunity to change its future

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: by giving mission-driven organizations, qualified entities, a meaningful chance to acquire the buildings and chart a different, non-speculative future for the families who live there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Congratulations, Councilmember Sandy Nurse, for your persistence and patience to get COPA across the finish line to the COPA Coalition, led by New Economy Project and the New York City Land Initiative, and tenant organizers across the city, including our Bronx in my neck of the woods.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: If you live in a nice private home with a front yard and a backyard, congrats, that's great.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But for those of us who represent communities who need our help, this is a critical tool in the arsenal.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Sorry I can't make the celebration, child care, but please celebrate for me.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And with that, I vote aye on all.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Aldebar.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shirley Aldebol explains her vote in favor of COPA, emphasizing the importance of preserving existing affordable housing. She also explains her support for Intro 943A, ending the horse carriage industry, while calling for accountability on worker transition.
chapters.title: Council Member Aldebol explains vote on COPA and horse carriage bill

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: First, I want to congratulate Council Member Sandy Nurse on her incredible hard work,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: coalition building, listening to the concerns of myself and others, and her perseverance in bringing COPA to a vote today.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: We rightly spend a significant amount of time on City Council discussing and working on how to build more affordable housing, but preserving existing affordable housing is just as impactful and vital to tackling the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'm excited to continue to work with this coalition, opportunities to expand affordable housing and not not-for-profit housing development organizations in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I'd also like to take a moment to explain my vote on Intro 943A, prohibiting the operation of horse-drawn cabs and establishing an industry transition plan.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: This bill has a unique and challenging intersection of issues for me.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Fundamentally, I believe that it is time to end the horse carriage industry due to the consumer and worker protection risks that it poses, in addition to the animal welfare concerns that it raises.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Recent tragic incidences have reinforced the risks that both passengers and drivers face while navigating horse carriages on an increasingly busy road.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: busy, unpredictable streets of New York City and Central Park.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I have a deep respect for workers and small business owners who have built their livelihood through the horse carriage business and the unions that fight for them.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Many have done this work for decades and come to it from a passion for animals and an interest in working with people.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I do appreciate the work of both Speaker Menon and Mayor Mamdani to incorporate transition planning commitments for affected workers and business owners into this legislation.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And I am optimistic that we will hold the administration accountable and ensure that the transition plans will include compensation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Council member, eligible?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I vote aye.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Ariola.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carmen De La Rosa discloses her daughter works for the Department of Education. She explains her vote in favor of Intro 943, arguing that protecting workers and animals are not competing values and that the city can do both.
chapters.title: Council Member De La Rosa explains vote on horse carriage bill

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: De La Rosa.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Well, I have to disclose that the Department of Education is on the agenda on the transparency resolution.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: My daughter is associated with the Department of Education.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: As the former chair of the Labor Committee in this body and as someone who has been in elected office for 10 years next year,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: in 2027, I've spent most of my public service fighting for workers'rights, and that commitment weighs heavy on me today.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But that commitment is also not to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I would not allow anyone to question my commitment to the workers of our city.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: So today, I am voting in favor of Intro 943 with the confidence

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: that we will ensure that workers will be protected and that there is a just transition that will be prioritized and that the safety and the rights of animals will also be ensured by this vote.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Because we can do all those things at once.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: After decades of debate and advocacy and hearings, the status quo is not serving anyone anymore.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: In June,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: 18-year-old tourist Romach Mahajan lost his life, and that is something that should bring pause to everyone.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Each incident endangers animals.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: the public workers whose lives depend on this industry.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: And tensions are high on every side of this issue, but delays serve none of us.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I support this legislation, and I know and do not take lightly what it means to close this chapter.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: But there is a genuine commitment from the people in this room to make sure that the livelihoods of those impacted

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: are prioritized.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Carriage drivers have built their lives on years of experience, specialized skills, and relationship with customers.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Many have paid out of pocket for medallions and equipment, and they are workers of our city, and they deserve to be treated as partners in this transition.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: We are committed to that.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I want to thank Chair Shulman, Speaker Menon,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: and all of our colleagues who have listened to the debate and come up with a fair and balanced solution.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Protecting workers and protecting animals are not competing values, and today we choose to do both.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: I also want to take a moment to thank Sandy Nurse for her courage, for her conviction,

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: for her balanced approach to ensuring that we are making a dent in the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Carmen N. De La Rosa
utterances.text: Thank you, and I proudly vote aye on all.

chapters.summary: Council Member Amanda Farías explains she cannot support Intro 943 because the transition plan lacks concrete commitments for workers. She votes aye on all other items, abstaining on Intro 943.
chapters.title: Council Member Farías abstains on horse carriage bill, supports COPA

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Farias.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Over the years, I've spoken with both animal welfare advocates and members of the horse carriage industry and workers union in hopes of finding a solution that addresses the concerns of all parties.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I believe we have a responsibility to both protect animal welfare while also ensuring that workers and their families are not left behind.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I do not believe this bill in its current form strikes that balance.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The proposed transition does not provide the concrete commitments to economic support, workforce retraining, and pathways to stable employment that the workers deserve.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And for me, 18 months is not a realistic time frame for any person or industry to transition into a new industry.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I cannot support a transition that leaves these questions and concerns unresolved, and I remain committed to working towards a solution that is fair, responsible, and considers everyone impacted.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Separately, and equally as important, congratulations to my colleague, Councilmember Nurse, for passing COPA.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: A long fight, and I'm really proud to see this pass today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This is the bill we need.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We knew that last session, and we know it now, so proud to be a sponsor and support of that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And with that, I vote aye on all with the exception of introduction 943, in which I abstain.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Oswald Feliz speaks in favor of the horse carriage ban, arguing that horses do not belong in a busy city and that the industry poses public safety risks. He also congratulates Council Member Nurse on COPA.
chapters.title: Council Member Feliz supports horse carriage ban and COPA

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So many big bills that we're voting on today.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Proud to vote aye on all.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm especially proud to vote aye on the COPA bill and also the horse carriage bill.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: On the horses, it is time to ban the horse carriages for many reasons.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: First, my colleague said it perfectly, this is not the 1800s anymore.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Second, these carriages, as we know, have created serious and escalating public safety threats for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Every single year, there's a new incident, a new accident.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These horses, as we know, are not meant to be in a loud and busy city like ours.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: They can panic and run unpredictably and uncontrollably with something as simple as a vehicle noise, as a garbage truck, something that is obviously common in a busy city like ours.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: These are issues that cannot be resolved through more training and more legislation.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I'm so glad that we're finally doing what is right and we're finally putting an end to these carriages.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're also doing it in a way that is responsible.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: We're making sure that there's a transition period for the workers and also making sure that the horses are also protected.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: So I just want to thank Speaker Menon and also Councilmember Marte, really good on making this bill and this idea a reality in the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Also briefly on COPA, I just want to congratulate Councilmember Nurse on getting that bill to the finish line.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: That was obviously not an easy bill.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I know all of us remember those very long conversations during meetings, including Democratic Conference.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: Obviously a very complicated issue.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: You worked tirelessly and diligently, and you left no stone unturned.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: did everything you needed to do to get that idea into reality, and make a lot of the city of New York, so congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Oswald J. Feliz
utterances.text: I vote aye on all.

utterances.speaker: James F. Gennaro
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shahana Hanif speaks in support of Romancia's law and COPA, praising the advocates and colleagues who fought for these bills. She votes aye on all.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif celebrates passage of horse carriage ban and COPA

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today I am proud that under Speaker Menon's leadership, this council is passing Ramach's law, ending the dangerous and inhumane horse-drawn carriage industry after nearly two decades of advocacy and struggle in these halls.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We must never forget the preventable injuries and deaths of horses and humans that occurred while our city failed to act.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: As vice co-chair of the Animal Welfare Caucus and a longtime sponsor of this legislation, I am deeply grateful for the advocates who never gave up.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Today we honor Ryder and Romach and take a historic step toward a safer, more humane city.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I also congratulate our fierce Progressive Caucus co-chair, Sandy Nurse, on passing COPA.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Councilmember Nurse and the New York City Community Land Initiative Coalition weathered a veto and a coordinated corporate disinformation campaign to reach this moment.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Six years in the making, this victory belongs to the countless New Yorkers who demanded real tools to fight private equity firms buying up our homes and displacing our communities.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I was proud to serve as Progressive Caucus co-chair when we adopted COPA as a priority last term.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: My colleagues and our movement stood strong through every fight.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: COPA is a major victory for housing justice and puts people before shareholder profits.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: With that, I vote aye on all.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Crystal Hudson congratulates Council Member Nurse on passing COPA, calling it a lifeline for communities facing displacement and systemic racism. She votes aye on all.
chapters.title: Council Member Hudson explains vote on COPA

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'd like to take a moment to congratulate my colleague, Councilmember Nurse, on passing COPA once again.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: This historic legislation is a critical step toward preserving affordable housing and protecting longtime New Yorkers from displacement.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I'm proud to have supported both iterations of this bill when it first passed, then when it was vetoed by the former mayor, and now as it passes this body again.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Despite the ups and downs from both sides of City Hall, Councilmember Nurse has remained a tireless and steadfast advocate for COPA and the communities it is designed to protect.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Councilmember Nurse is not only an exemplary public servant and advocate, she is a true organizer.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: She cares deeply for her community, and her commitment is why this bill has endured.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: COPA represents an important shift away from speculative investment and toward the community preservation and long-term affordability New Yorkers deserve.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For those of us who represent communities that have been subjected to unsafe and inhabitable living conditions, COPA is a lifeline.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For those of us who represent communities that have been denied opportunities to purchase property because of systemic racism, COPA is a lifeline.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: For those of us who represent communities struggling to afford rent every single day, COPA is a lifeline, and today I'm proud to be part of delivering that lifeline to our constituents.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Congratulations and thank you, Councilmember Nurse and all of the advocates who have

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: have fought so hard for so long.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Eye on all.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Rita Joseph speaks in support of COPA, sharing stories from her district of tenants suffering from neglectful landlords. She argues COPA will keep buildings affordable and in community hands.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph explains vote on COPA

utterances.text: Joseph.

utterances.text: I vote aye.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: In January, when COPA fell short, I told tenants of District 40 that the fight was not over.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today, we keep that promise.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to thank Councilmember Nurse for never backing down, for years of negotiating, listening, and refusing to let this bill die.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you to the tenant organizers, the community land trust, and the advocates who kept showing up.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you to the speaker and the mayor for helping bring COPA home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Let me tell you why this matters.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Flatbush and Prospect Park, Lefferts Garden and Dittmas Park, Crown Heights, my office take calls, no heat in January, mold in a baby's bedroom, ceilings coming down, repairs promised and never made.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Too many of our constituents live in buildings owned by landlords who treat their homes as a line on a spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And when those buildings are sold, they often go to developers and the cycle starts all over again.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: COPA breaks that cycle.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: When a distressed building goes up for sale, mission-driven non-for-profits and community land trusts will finally get a fair shot at buying it and keeping it affordable, safe, and in the hands of the community.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: As a forever educator, I know for more than two decades, I learned that a child cannot learn without a stable home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And this is what's at stake for the families in these buildings.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And that is why COPA matter.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Housing is not.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Not a commodity.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It is a home.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I probably vote iron.

utterances.text: I commend the Speaker Menon's leadership of this council after 19 years of our body not taking action on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thanks to the advocates and a big thank you to Speaker Menon for standing up to get this done finally.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I also want to commend, we passed a number of bills today, I also want to commend Councilman Bersandi-Nurse on our passage of COPA, also a long time in the coming, but as a former housing lawyer,

utterances.text: myself, I know how it's not just about building new housing, but it's about preserving affordable housing and combating displacement.

chapters.summary: Council Member Frank Morano explains his vote in favor of Intro 943A, acknowledging that reasonable people disagree. He believes horses are not machines and that ending the industry is necessary, while also supporting transition assistance for workers.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Mealy.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Moranil.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader, for recognizing me.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to briefly explain my vote today in favor of Intro 943A because I recognize that this is an issue on which reasonable people, including people I respect enormously, can disagree.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: A lot of my friends in organized labor oppose the legislation, so do some of my fellow Republicans.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And I understand their concerns about protecting jobs and preserving traditions and respecting the people who've built their livelihoods around this industry.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And those concerns deserve to be taken seriously.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I don't believe every carriage driver mistreats animals.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I believe a lot of drivers genuinely care about their horses and take pride in their work.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: But horses are living animals.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: They're not machines.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Even a healthy, well-trained horse can become frightened and react unpredictably.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You can regulate human behavior, but you can't regulate away animal instinct in the streets of Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The tragic death of 18-year-old Romach Mahajan brought that reality into particularly sharp focus.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: He came to New York City with his family to celebrate his high school graduation and the beginning of his college education.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Instead, his family suffered.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: unimaginable loss.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also recognize that ending an industry has real consequences for the people employed in it, and these workers deserve meaningful transition assistance, employment opportunities, and fair treatment.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Those responsibilities don't disappear with today's vote, and I'm eager to work with my colleagues on helping these folks.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: And the horses deserve responsible, humane retirement arrangements.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I believe it's possible to respect the people who work in an industry while conceding and concluding that the industry itself should come to an end.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to particularly recognize our former colleague, former council member Bob Holden, who championed this legislation long before today's vote.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: His years of work deserve acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I also want to thank Speaker Menon for her leadership and all the advocates, including the man who should be mayor, Curtis Lewa.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: With that, I saw how quick the majority leader was to cut me off.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: With that, I will vote aye on all with the exception of Intro 786A, Intro 905A, and Reso 695, on which I vote no.

utterances.text: Today we are tackling multiple issues that have been debated in the halls of New York City government for decades.

utterances.text: It is long overdue that we ban horse carriages in Central Park, and I want to commend everyone for their hard work on getting this over the finish line.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson speaks in favor of Intro 943A, describing horses suffering in Hell's Kitchen. He also supports COPA, praising Council Member Nurse's tenacity. He votes aye on all.

utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson

chapters.summary: Council Member David Carr explains his vote against COPA and Intro 943A, citing his commitment to private property rights and free enterprise. He argues that ending the horse carriage industry is not justified and hopes for a dignified transition for workers.
chapters.title: Council Member Carr explains no votes on COPA and horse carriage bill

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Permission to explain my vote?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Permission granted.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Make sure the minority leader gets five minutes.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I joined government and sought to join government years ago because I had a passionate commitment to both the right to private property as well as to our free enterprise system.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Private property because history has shown that it is a critical cornerstone to our system of political and economic rights.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And the free market because while imperfect, it is the best proven way of bringing the most prosperity to the most people.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I'll be voting against the new version of COPPA today because it limits the rights of property owners.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It may be a circumstance where I have great sympathy for the tenants in the buildings that will be

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: covered by this legislation and I have very little sympathy for the owners who are selling, but our political rights are sacrosanct and that

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That doesn't change based on the sympathy I have for the individuals who possess them.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That's the whole point of these political rights, is to ensure that everyone has access to them regardless of our opinion of them and the circumstances in which they're availing themselves of it.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And similarly, I cannot in good conscience vote in favor of Intro 943A.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: This is the council ending a particular means of employment.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And colleagues invoked earlier, you know, other forms of employment, other ways of earning a living that once existed in our city and no longer do.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The examples given, like the milk delivery person, these are jobs that disappeared because of advances in employment and technology, rather, or because of changes in the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Unlike, for example, the one my great-grandparents worked in, which was the fur coat industry, they labored in the garment district here in Manhattan in the Depression era.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That was an industry that was ended in New York City by the council.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So I cannot in good conscience support an end to this particular means of work and livelihood for so many New Yorkers when it is no more dangerous than the other means of getting around our city.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Getting around New York City is dangerous, whether it's by car, by for-hire vehicle, by bus, by bike, or other means, even horse carriages.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And when there are issues that need to be addressed in terms of safety, we address them through regulation as we have done.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so I do hope that since the bill appears a poison,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: to pass today that the commitments that have been articulated here and before today about finding an opportunity for these folks, owners and workers, to continue to earn a living in a way that keeps them

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: in the life to which they are accustomed, in a way that keeps them in having dignity in the workplace and in their home.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I hope that we...

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Meet those expectations.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so that being said, I vote no on intros 786A, 905A, 943B, and pre-considered resolution 695, and I on the rest.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.
