utterances.text: Keep it quiet.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: If you wish to vote against or abstain from any of today's resolutions, please notify the Legislative Documents Unit by email or by approaching the dais.

chapters.summary: The Council holds a voice vote on Resolution 625B, which declares October as Reggaeton Heritage Month. The ayes have it.
chapters.title: Voice vote on Resolution 625B declaring October Reggaeton Heritage Month

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll now read today's resolutions into the record.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Resolution 625B declares October as Reggaeton Heritage Month in the City of New York to honor the legacy of reggaeton as a prominent expression

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: of Afro-Caribbean and Latin American identity and to recognize New York's pivotal role in facilitating the blend of cultures that is at the heart of this grassroots musical genre.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All those in favor say aye.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All opposed say nay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Any abstentions?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The ayes have it.

chapters.summary: The Council holds a voice vote on Resolution 650, which opposes the federal rule change on Head Start programs. The ayes have it.
chapters.title: Voice vote on Resolution 650 opposing federal Head Start rule change

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Resolution 650 opposes the federally proposed rule change titled Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs and calling on the federal government to prioritize protecting and growing access to high-quality education for young children.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All those in favor say aye.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All opposed say nay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Any abstentions?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The ayes have it.

chapters.summary: Council Member Kayla Santosuosso introduces the Stop Super Speeders bill, which requires speed limiting devices for drivers with 16 or more speeding violations in school zones. She also introduces legislation to prevent TLC-issued vehicles from using flock surveillance technology.
chapters.title: Council Member Santosuosso introduces Stop Super Speeders bill and TLC surveillance bill

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now move into general discussion.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have eight folks signed up so far.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Santos Suoso, followed by Hanif.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Today, I was proud to introduce the Stop Super Speeders Bill, which completes a process started by,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: thank you, which completes a process started in the state by State Senator Andrew Gernardis and Assemblymember Emily Gallagher,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: which would require the installation of speed limiting devices in vehicles where the drivers have incurred 16

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: or more speeding violations in school zones and caught on camera within 12 months.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: This is an important street safety bill.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And as someone who both walks and rides a bike and drives a car, I just want to clarify that this is a bill that keeps our streets safe for everybody and cracks down on our worst offenders

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: and is not targeted at anybody who, you know, gets one or two speeding tickets, as I'm sure many in this chamber have gotten.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so I look to finally complete this process started by those leaders in the state by passing this bill and fully implementing the Stop Super Speeders bill.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And I encourage my colleagues to sign on, and I'll be circling around with you soon about that.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I also introduced legislation today to prevent TLC-issued vehicles from using flock surveillance-based technology, and I will be speaking with each of you about that soon.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And thank you to everybody that held my baby today.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shahana Hanif introduces Intro 1137, a three-year initiative to support businesses owned by New Yorkers with disabilities in every borough. She also honors two constituents who recently passed away.
chapters.title: Council Member Hanif introduces bill to support businesses owned by New Yorkers with disabilities

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Hanif, followed by Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm proud to introduce Introduction 1137 legislation that's already earned the support of 10 of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: This bill would establish a three-year initiative to support businesses owned and operated by New Yorkers with disabilities with a brick-and-mortar

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: location in every borough and annual reporting to measure its impact.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The initiative would be administered by the Department of Small Businesses in coordination with the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities and NYC Talent.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Too often, New Yorkers with disabilities face barriers not only to finding employment, but to creating businesses, building wealth, and becoming job creators themselves.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Economic justice for people with disabilities must mean more than access to jobs.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It must also mean access to ownership, entrepreneurship, and economic power.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to sign on.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I want to honor the lives of two remarkable women from my district in Kensington, Tassine Ferdos and Zainab Ahmed, who tragically passed away this week.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Both were my constituents and childhood classmates at PS230.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: We are the same age.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: They died too young at 35.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Tassine was a beloved educator and classical dancer who touched the countless lives through her teaching and artistry.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Zainab was a dedicated public servant and talented artist whose work was just exhibited.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I just saw her.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Both women gave so much to our city and our communities, and their sudden passing is heartbreaking.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: My deepest condolences go out to their families, friends, and everyone whose lives they touched.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: May they both rest in peace.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

chapters.summary: Council Member Farah Louis introduces Intro 1146, which requires annual reporting on DYCD fiscal agent performance, and Intro 1147, which requires public disclosure of MWBE disparity studies and underlying data.
chapters.title: Council Member Louis introduces bills on DYCD fiscal agents and MWBE disparity studies

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Lewis, followed by Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Today I'm introducing two bills.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: The first, Intro 1146, addresses the performance of fiscal agents contracted by the Department of Youth and Community Development, DYCD, to manage funds on behalf of community-based organizations.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: These organizations provide critical services to our young people and neighborhoods, but delays in payments and administrative challenges can interfere with their ability to deliver.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: This bill requires DYCD to report annually on fiscal agent performance and establish a feedback mechanism for organizations to raise concerns.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Also, I'm introducing Intro 1147, which requires the Department of Small Business Services to publicly disclose MWBE disparity studies and their underlying data.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Minority and women-owned businesses continue to face barriers in competing for city contracts.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Making these studies and their data publicly available will strengthen transparency and help us to better understand disparities

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: in contracting and whether our participation goals reflect the realities these businesses face.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: I urge...

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: my colleagues to support these bills.

utterances.speaker: Farah N. Louis
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer introduces Intro 1132 for a Landmarks Preservation Commission public records portal, Intro 1133 for a stipulated fine program for small businesses, and a bill for a study on gambling behaviors and casino impacts. She also introduces resolutions on cryptocurrency kiosks and anti-aging product warning labels.
chapters.title: Council Member Brewer introduces Landmarks portal, small business fines, and gambling study bills

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilor Brewer and final is Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm introducing intro 1132, a public record portal for the Landmarks Preservation Commission.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: 38,000 landmark properties every year and there's no portal where members of the public can access all of the records and there are 12

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: thousand applications, so we need the portal.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, 1133, the stipulated fine and commercial abatement program needs to apply to small businesses.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We know that large businesses get a stipulated

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: abatement program for their fines and we wanted to apply to the smaller stores and we have some ways of doing that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Last year collected 58.3 million for 776,000 fines.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number three is a study of gambling behaviors and the impact of casino

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Openings, getting the Department of Health and Mental Health to study gambling behaviors and the impact of casino openings.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Two resolutions, one to regulate cryptocurrency kiosks and another one to require anti-aging.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Products to contain a warning label and we have a list of those that should be included and there's a resolution in Albany regarding the same topic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I hope you sign on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Council Member Carl Wilson introduces resolutions commemorating fashion designer Bob Mackie and music icon Dolly Parton, highlighting their contributions to culture and New York City. He notes Dolly Parton received the key to the city in 1978.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson honors Bob Mackie and Dolly Parton

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Council Member Wilson, followed by Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I know we have a busy day today, but I'd like to end with something a little lighter.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I'm honored to be introducing resolutions commemorating two recently departed icons who left an indelible mark on popular culture in this city, this country, and the world.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: With the passing of fashion designer Bob Mackie on September 14th, the world lost a unique artist's talent whose work is woven into the fabric of this city.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Mackie pioneered bold looks.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: From his workshop on 7th Avenue, Mackie created pieces of high glamour not only for Hollywood stars, but for the working women of New York.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: His 60-year career demonstrates the power of unapologetic camp and this city's enduring status as a trendsetter.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: On August 25th, Dolly Parton passed away at the age of 80, prompting an outpouring of grief and remembrance from admirers from around the world who celebrated her extraordinary contributions to music, philanthropy, business, literature, and American culture.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Workers of the world united through Dolly's melodies.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: With a syncopated clicking of nails on a typewriter at the start of 9 to 5, she made relatable despair over white-collar drudgery catchy.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Coat of Many Colors spoke to the beauty amidst the struggle found in working-class life, her remarkable leadership in literacy,

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: initiatives and philanthropy further showed that working people and the disadvantaged were never far from her heart.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: My resolution, 702, honors her contributions to the world and connection to New York City.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Those included being presented with the key of the city of New York in 1978.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: So in this chamber, I hope everyone will join me in telling Dolly that New York City will always love you.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Council Member Rita Joseph introduces Intro 1144, which requires a full analysis of gender-based violence data across the city, including disparities by race, ethnicity, sex, and gender. She urges colleagues to sign on.
chapters.title: Council Member Joseph introduces Intro 1144 for gender-based violence data analysis

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Joseph.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader and Madam Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Colleagues, we're standing here in the final days of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: All month long, we've worn purple, we've held vigils, and we've said the names of New Yorkers we've lost.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Today, I want to do something more than the last thing than remember.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want us to measure.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That's why I'm proud to introduce Intro 1144 along colleagues, Councilmember Farias and Councilmember Lewis.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Right now, the Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence reports to this council every year.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It tells us how many people walk through the doors of our family justice centers, how many trainings were held, how many outreach events took place.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: That information matters.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: But it tells us what we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It doesn't tell us enough about what survivors are facing.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Intro 1144 changes that, beginning in January of 2028 and every two years after.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And domestic gender-based violence, we'll publish a full analysis of gender-based violence across our city, including complaints, arrests, and outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: And it will show us the disparities by race, by ethnicity, by sex, and by gender.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Because we know violence doesn't land evenly.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Black women, immigrant women, trans New Yorkers, they too often face the most harm and the fewer doors that are open.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I learned you cannot help a student if you refuse to see.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: The same is true for our city.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: If we want to direct resources where they are needed the most, we need the full picture.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Data is not the end of this work.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: It is how we do this work, honestly.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I want to thank my staff, the advocates, and survivors who pushed for this.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: I urge my colleagues to sign on.

utterances.speaker: Rita C. Joseph
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

summary: The NYC Council held a stated meeting on October 22, 2026, passing Romancia's law to phase out horse-drawn carriages by 2028 and the Community Opportunity to Purchase Act (COPA) to preserve affordable housing.

The Council also voted to raise the SCRI/DRI income eligibility limit to $75,000, and approved numerous other bills and resolutions on topics including ballot access in jails, special education reporting, gender-based violence data, and street renaming.

The meeting included a failed amendment to extend the horse carriage phase-out to 2030, extensive debate on COPA and the horse carriage ban, and the introduction of new bills on disability-owned businesses, speed limiters, and domestic violence data.
title: Stated Meeting
